name: PT Pelayaran Nasional Bina Buana Raya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bina Buana Raya: a coal-barge and AHTS operator priced for a trough
frontmatter.summary: BBRM charters self-propelled barges to coal shippers and anchor-handling vessels to oil and gas operators. A new AHTS joins a net-cash balance sheet while the shares trade below book and near a multi-year low. The market prices no contribution from the new vessel; we think a full year of it plus a peer re-rating is the most likely path. BUY.
thesis: The AHTS MP Maverick was bought for US$12.1m against an independent appraisal of Rp230.9 billion, and it was delivered after the last reported balance sheet; our forecast gives it a full year only from FY2027E [S4, F25, F30].
At Rp93 the shares trade at 8.6x forward earnings, 0.9x book and 4.6x EBITDA, against a peer median of 7.4 EBITDA for the direct coal-logistics comparables [S0].

The P&L is taxed under the final shipping regime at a small fraction of revenue, so almost all operating profit reaches cash; capex falls away after the vessel payment and no dividend is paid, compounding net cash [S2].
The balance sheet is already net cash and the debt taken for the new vessel is matched by an asset independently appraised above its purchase price [S0, S4].
The bear case is a regional OSV supply wave, weaker coal trade and an equity raise; even then the twelve-month value is Rp124 against Rp93, so the asymmetry is favourable [S2, S0].

catalysts.event: AHTS MP Maverick delivered and available for charter; first revenue in Q4-2026
First full quarter of AHTS operation and FY2027 charter cover announcements
FY2026 audited results against the revenue and net-profit targets
2027 RKAB coal quota approval, the main swing factor for domestic barge volumes

blocks.text: **Rating BUY, twelve-month target Rp158, 70.0% expected return.** The target is the probability-weighted value of our three scenarios after a 10.0% discount for the thin free float, and it sits against a Rp93 share price. The primary method is a ten-year discounted cash-flow at a 11.5% WACC and a 2.0% terminal growth rate; the EV/EBITDA and P/B cross-checks sit below it once an outlier comparable is removed, and the valuation section reconciles the gap rather than claiming three methods agree [S0, S2].

The variant view is simple. BBRM is a small Indonesian shipowner with two books: self-propelled barges that carry coal, and anchor-handling tug supply vessels chartered to oil and gas operators [S2]. It reported US$13.8m of revenue and US$6.3m of net profit in FY2025, ended the year with more cash than debt, and has since taken delivery of a large AHTS bought for US$12.1m — a price the company says sits below an independent appraisal [S0, S2, S4]. The shares, however, have fallen from a speculative peak and now trade below book and at a mid-single-digit EBITDA multiple [S0].

What the market appears to price is the company without the new vessel. Our reverse DCF says today's price implies FY2027 revenue growth of 1.7% against the 10.4% we forecast; that solve holds the discount rate, terminal growth and payout at our assumptions, so it is an illustration of the gap rather than a verdict — but it indicates the market attributes little value to the new vessel [S0]. That gap is what the thesis is built on. The two or three things that move the value are the day rate and utilisation achieved by the new AHTS, the coal trade that sets barge demand, and whether the group converts its cash into distributions or further fleet renewal [S2, S4].

BBRM is PT Pelayaran Nasional Bina Buana Raya Tbk, a Jakarta-based shipowner with two operating segments: self-propelled barges (SPB) hired to coal shippers, and offshore support vessels (OSV) — specifically anchor-handling tug supply vessels — chartered to oil and gas companies on time charter [S2]. In FY2025 the OSV segment produced US$11.8m of revenue and the SPB segment US$2.0m [S2, F16, F17]. The charter book is several times the size of the barge book, so it is OSV utilisation and day rates, not coal freight, that set group earnings [S2]. Segment gross profit told the same story: OSV remains the profit engine while the barge book is smaller and more cyclical [S2].

The OSV fleet numbered four AHTS vessels at the FY2025 report date, and the company was acquiring one more, completed after the reporting period [S2, F21]. The SPB fleet was reshaped twice: a new barge bought in September 2024 and an older one, Premium Bahari, sold in October 2025 [S2]. That buy-new-sell-old pattern is the stated strategy — divesting older, lower-value tonnage and replacing it with higher-value vessels [S2]. The fleet operates across Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, so charter income is exposed to regional, not just domestic, oil and gas activity [S2].

The new vessel is the pivot of the story. It was bought for US$12.1m against an independent appraiser's market value of Rp230.9 billion at 28 September 2026, and the purchase was funded by a Rp120.0 billion investment loan from Bank IBK [S4, F25, F30, F31]. Against equity of US$44.3m, that is a material transaction for a company of this size, and it takes the AHTS fleet from the four vessels counted in the annual report to five [S2, F21, S4]. Unlike the barge book, the AHTS earns a daily charter rate under a time charter, so its contribution depends on utilisation and the day rate rather than on tonnes moved [S2]. No charter party or fixture for the new vessel is disclosed — the announcement says only that it has been handed over and is ready for operations [S4] — so rather than assume a spot rate we value it at the FY2025 fleet-average rate implied by disclosed actuals: OSV revenue of US$11.8m earned by four AHTS at 82.1% utilisation equates to a daily rate we apply to the new ship at the same utilisation [S2, F16, F18, F21]. That is the line that carries the FY2027 step-up, and the revenue-growth sensitivity grid is where a lower day rate would show.

Customers are oil and gas operators and coal shippers. Revenue concentration is high: the company discloses that two customers each accounted for more than a tenth of net revenue in FY2025, and one of the named counterparties is an international oilfield-services contractor [S2]. Management's FY2026 plan, set at the start of the year, targets US$14.2m of revenue, US$7.6m of direct expense and US$5.0m of net profit [S2, F22-F24]. The plan was set while the AHTS was expected to complete by mid-2026, so it already embeds a second-half vessel contribution [S2 p.19]; delivery slipped to October 2026, which leaves that contribution back-end loaded, but we hold FY2026E at the plan rather than adding a stub on top of it [S0, S2, S4].

Control is concentrated. PT Marcopolo Indonesia holds 70.7%, with Nam Cheong Pioneer and PT Sinar Bintang Makmur as the other substantial holders and the public holding 9.2% [S2 p.22]. The ultimate parent is SGX-listed Marco Polo Marine Ltd, and the controlling shareholders are named as Latip, Lie Ly and Sean Lee Yun Feng [S2 p.36]. The free float is correspondingly small, which is why the engine applies a liquidity discount and why daily traded value is a binding constraint for institutional money [S0, S2].

Coal barge operators sit between the mine and the export terminal: they load at a jetty or transhipment anchorage and deliver to a mother vessel, earning a freight rate per tonne that depends on distance, draft, waiting time and the coal price cycle. Offshore support vessels are the workhorses of offshore oil and gas, moving anchors, supplies, drilling equipment and crews; their day rates and utilisation follow the offshore capex cycle with a lag. Both are asset-heavy, cash-generative businesses in the upswing and cyclical in the downswing, which is why the balance sheet and the age profile of the fleet matter as much as the P&L.

The coal book is a function of Indonesian coal volumes and prices. Coal still supplies the majority of the country's power generation — the company cites two-thirds of plants — and the government approved a national production quota of around 700 Mt for 2026 [S2, S7, F27]. The high-calorie reference price was US$127/t in the second half of October 2026, recovering from the prior period but still below the July peak [S6, F26]. For a barge operator the relevant variable is not the absolute price but the volume moving from mine to port; a large quota and stable prices support barge demand even when prices are softer than the export peak [S7]. The quota has not, however, protected this operator's barge line: in 1H2026 SPB revenue fell 69.2% year on year to US$0.4m while OSV revenue rose to US$6.2m, the overwhelming majority of the total [S4]. The older barge Premium Bahari was sold in October 2025 [S2], so part of the decline is fleet rotation; the rest is weaker coal freight. We therefore treat the barge book as shrinking and cyclical, not as a floor.

The OSV book follows the offshore oil and gas cycle. The company describes an upturn in 2025 driven by global exploration and production, particularly deepwater, which lifted both utilisation and charter rates, and reports fleet utilisation of 82.1% [S2, F18]. Indonesia's policy backdrop is supportive: the government is targeting national production of a million barrels of oil per day and a large increase in gas output, and the local-content rule favours Indonesian-flagged tonnage in domestic contracts [S2]. Those are the drivers behind the OSV segment's pricing power, and they sit alongside the oil deck's Brent path of US$84.0/bbl [deck].

The coal link in our model is deliberately asymmetric. BBRM buys no coal — its cost of revenue is crew, fuel, depreciation, insurance, spares and agency fees — so the Newcastle benchmark is carried at a zero cost share; coal prices reach the P&L only through barge demand and tariffs, which sit in our revenue growth path [S2]. Brent enters through bunker fuel, which was about a tenth of FY2025 cost of revenue, with no fuel-surcharge clause disclosed, so fuel is a genuine margin exposure [S2, F19]. The coal deck's Newcastle path of US$118/t is therefore a demand indicator for the barge book rather than a direct price input [deck].

Across both books the economics are volume times spread, not commodity price times reserve. Barge revenue depends on the flow of coal from mine to port and on the freight rate per tonne, which is set by distance, draft and waiting time; OSV revenue depends on the number of vessels on hire and the day rate they earn [S2]. Coal prices therefore matter through the demand they generate for transport, and oil prices matter through the fuel the fleet burns, which is why the model carries Newcastle at a zero cost share and Brent at the bunker share [S2, F19]. That distinction is the difference between BBRM and the coal miners we cover: a weaker coal price can sit alongside a strong barge market if volume holds, and a stronger coal price does not by itself lift the freight rate [S2, S7].

Competition is fragmented. The coal-barge market has several listed and private operators with larger fleets; BBRM is a challenger with a handful of vessels, differentiated by a young fleet, an Indonesian flag and long-standing relationships with oil and gas charterers [S2]. Its moat is modest: vessels are fungible, barriers are capital and permits rather than technology, and charterers can switch on price. What it does have is a specialised AHTS capability, a regional operating footprint and the local-content advantage that comes with an Indonesian flag [S2]. Customer concentration cuts both ways — two customers above a tenth of revenue each is a real bargaining disadvantage — and the related-party share of charter revenue adds a governance dimension we return to under governance [S2].

The five forces are mixed. Supplier power is low, buyer power is high, the threat of new entrants is moderate, substitution is low for offshore work, and rivalry is high but currently tempered by a tight OSV market [S2]. The structural risk is the cycle: an OSV supply wave typically arrives two to four years after rates peak, and the sector has a long history of ordering at the top.

The record is one of steady revenue and volatile profit. Revenue rose from US$10.5m in FY2023 to US$13.4m in FY2024 and US$13.8m in FY2025, while net profit moved from US$4.0m to US$8.2m and then US$6.3m [S3, S2]. The swing is not operating leverage in the usual sense: the gross margin has held in the high forties across the period, and the profit variation comes from other income, finance costs and the one-off items we strip out [S2, S3].

FY2025 revenue was US$13.8m, up 2.9% on FY2024, with a gross margin of 48.1% and net profit of US$6.3m [S2, S0]. The revenue mix is heavily weighted to OSV, and the SPB line grew while OSV was broadly flat, reflecting the new barge bought in late 2024 [S2, F16, F17]. Operating expenses were US$1.2m; the reported operating profit includes an other-income line that we strip out of the base case because it was composed of foreign-exchange gains, receivable recoveries, an asset-disposal gain and a write-off of related-party payables [S2].

**The data pack's depreciation is wrong and we have restated it.** Yahoo's direct-cash-flow extraction carries D&A of a few thousand dollars, while the notes to the FY2025 accounts show total depreciation of US$2.0m allocated across cost of revenue and operating expenses [S0, S2, F7]. The pack's EBITDA of US$7.5m therefore understates the true figure once the LK charge is added back; on the restated numbers EBITDA is materially higher and EV/EBITDA correspondingly lower [S2, F7]. This is the single most important data correction in the model, and it is why the shares looked far more expensive on a naive screen than they are.

Our forecast follows the company's own plan for FY2026 and then the vessel arithmetic. FY2026E revenue of US$14.2m, 3.0% growth, is the company target as printed [S2, F22], which already embeds the AHTS contribution assumed for the second half [S2 p.19]; we add no stub on top of it, with a gross margin of 44.2% — the target's own revenue and direct-expense arithmetic adjusted for the fuel-cost link while Brent trades above our long-run base price [S2, F23, deck]. FY2027E revenue of US$15.7m adds the full year of the vessel at the FY2025 fleet-average day rate and utilisation, net of the half-year already embedded in the plan, worth 10.4% above FY2026 [S2, S4, F16, F18, F21]; thereafter growth settles at 3.0% to 3.0%, USD inflation, because no rate-escalation or utilisation source exists beyond the vessel year and no further fleet expansion is sourced [S2].

Margins hold rather than expand. Gross margin recovers to 46.0% and operating expenses stay near 8.5% of revenue, in line with FY2025 actuals and the company target [S2]. D&A rises to 15.5% of revenue when the new vessel is in service, and capex falls from 39.6% of revenue in FY2026 — the year of the remaining vessel payment — to 13.5% of sustaining and dry-docking spend [S2, S4, F25]. The company had paid the majority of the purchase price by December 2025, so FY2026 carries only the balance plus docking, not the whole price [S2 p.54]. Thereafter replacement capex is held at the D&A ratio, because a fleet depreciating at that rate needs replacement spend at least equal to the charge [S2, F13]. The direction of travel is consistent with what management reported at the January 2026 public expose, where the nine-month EBITDA margin was put at 61.0%, up from the prior-year period [S5]. The model's FY2026E EBITDA margin of 50.0% sits below the FY2025 actual of 54.3%, and the bridge is sourced rather than asserted: the company plan itself budgets a higher direct-expense ratio, and so a lower gross margin, than FY2025 achieved, and the spot-Brent bunker link adds fuel cost while Brent trades above our deck price [S2, deck]. The first-half gross margin was above the full-year forecast, so the gap may prove conservative; we carry it openly rather than hiding it.

The first half of 2026 kept the company on the run-rate implied by the annual target. Revenue was close to half the full-year plan and the balance sheet stayed in net cash after the drawdown on the vessel facility, but the segment mix was not stable: barge revenue fell 69.2% year on year to US$0.4m while the OSV book grew [S0, S4]. Net profit in the first half was already the majority of the full-year plan, and the company beat its FY2025 net-profit plan by US$2.2m [S0, S2]. We treat the plan as a floor, not a ceiling, and hold FY2026E at the plan as printed, which already carries the vessel's second-half contribution, rather than extrapolating the first-half profit run-rate [S0, S2]. The cash-flow consequence is the point: with capex concentrated in the vessel year, free cash flow is temporarily negative in FY2026E at US$1.5m and swings to US$5.8m in FY2027E, which is what a fleet-renewal year looks like rather than a deterioration in the business [S0]. From FY2027E the cash conversion is high because the final tax takes a small fraction of revenue and no distribution is paid [S2].

The balance sheet is a strength. At end-FY2025 cash was US$12.4m against debt of US$3.2m, a net cash position, and even after the June 2026 drawdown for the vessel the group remained net cash [S0, S2, F15]. Net debt to EBITDA is negative in our forecast throughout, and the final shipping tax regime means the tax line is small relative to profit — a structural cash-conversion advantage for Indonesian-flagged charter income [S2]. Working capital runs at about a fifth of revenue, consistent with receivables from charterers, and we hold that ratio [S0, S2].

Capital allocation has been reinvestment, not distribution. The company has paid no dividend in the years covered by the price history and explicitly declared none for FY2025; retained earnings have gone into vessel renewal [S0, S2]. But the arithmetic has changed: the fleet programme is loan-funded, capex falls after the vessel year, and the group is in net cash [S0, S4]. The 23 June 2026 AGM nevertheless resolved to pay no FY2025 dividend and to allocate the profit to fleet procurement [S10], so we carry a nil payout in the base case, matching the actual; a distribution remains upside capacity, not a modelled input. The dividend-capacity test at through-cycle free cash flow is the anchor to watch: FY2027E free cash flow of US$5.8m on a net-cash balance sheet would support a distribution if the board chose one [S0, S2]. The group has used rights issues historically — the pre-emptive offerings of the last decade are in the company history — so any future fleet programme that is equity-funded would be a per-share risk, not merely a balance-sheet event [S2], and the bear scenario carries exactly that dilution.

**Earnings-quality flags.** The accruals picture is mixed, not clean. Operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025, and the three-year accruals ratio — net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets — averages close to zero, so the P&L is broadly cash-backed [S0, S2]. But trade receivables rose from US$2.6m to US$3.3m while revenue grew only marginally, several times faster than sales and well past the house card's receivables-divergence trigger; receivables now represent several months of billings [S0, S2]. We hold working capital at 20.0% of revenue, which leaves a collection allowance in the bear case rather than the base; a further build would be the first sign of slower charter collections. The other optics flag is the extension of vessel useful lives from twenty to twenty-five years in 2025, which reduced the depreciation charge; it is disclosed and small, but it flatters margins modestly and we note it rather than adjust for it [S2]. Related-party charter revenue was a material minority of the total in FY2025, and FY2024 other income included a gain on writing off related-party payables — the modal value-transfer channel on IDX and a governance item, not an accounting error [S2, F20]. Customer concentration and the thin free float are the other two structural flags [S2, S0].

We value BBRM primarily on a ten-year FCFF DCF. A charter operator is a capital-asset business whose value is the discounted stream of charter cash flows net of the capex needed to keep the fleet in class, so a cash-flow model with explicit vessel economics fits better than a spot-earnings multiple [S2]. The DCF is anchored on the last actual year and the company's FY2026 target, with the new vessel's full-year contribution from FY2027E and no volume or margin uplift beyond what is sourced [S2, S4].

The cost of capital is built bottom-up: a risk-free rate of 5.0%, an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.00 (the industry default for transport), a debt weight of 14.0% and a pre-tax cost of debt of 7.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 12.5% and a WACC of 11.5%. Terminal growth is 2.0%, roughly long-run dollar inflation, because no further fleet expansion is sourced [S2].

Two cautions on the discount rate. The engine derives the debt weight from gross debt over market capitalisation, while the company is in net cash [S0]; it also uses a pre-tax cost of debt equal to the risk-free rate plus the macro corporate spread, below the 9.0% the model itself charges on the IDR vessel loan, and a statutory tax shield although the company pays the final shipping tax [S0, S2]. The WACC is therefore a source of value-ward bias. We have not edited the engine: the sensitivity table shows the DCF at higher discount rates, and at the cost of equity alone the DCF is materially lower than the headline. We flag the absent target-leverage override for OPS.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$64.4m, of which 43.7% is terminal value, and an equity value per share of Rp152 after adding net cash [S0, S2]. The terminal share is moderate for a shipping name, so the value is not a terminal-value artefact [S0].

The cross-checks use a curated peer set of the direct coal-logistics and Indonesian-flag shipping comparables rather than the full industry table, which mixes unrelated and near-zero-EBITDA names [S0]. We exclude MBSS because its multiple sits on a thin EBITDA base and alone sets the multi-name medians: it would pin both cross-checks to a single outlier [S0]. On the retained names the EV/EBITDA median is struck on three (PSSI carries no EV/EBITDA multiple in the pack) and the P/B median on four, producing Rp133 and Rp150 respectively. Both sit below the DCF and we explain the gap rather than claim convergence [S0].

Two cautions apply to the multiple. The comparables are small caps whose EBITDA bases are thin, so a single contract win or loss moves their multiples far more than it moves ours; we use medians rather than means and do not extend the set to the wider shipping universe, where capital structure and contract type differ [S0]. The cross-check is also mechanical: it applies the peer median to our FY2025A EBITDA of US$7.5m, the last actual year, in which the new vessel does not contribute at all; on a forward EBITDA that includes the vessel the multiple would produce a higher value. The lower cross-check is therefore a floor struck on the pre-vessel earnings base, which is one reason the DCF carries half the weight [S0].

Sensitivity to WACC and terminal growth is shown below. The value is more sensitive to the discount rate than to growth, as expected for a long-duration cash-flow asset; a one-percentage-point higher WACC takes the DCF value down by roughly a tenth, and a lower one lifts it by a similar amount [S0].

What does today's price imply? The reverse DCF says the market is pricing FY2027 revenue growth of 1.7% against our 10.4% [S0]. That is a single-variable solve: WACC, terminal growth and payout are held at our assumptions, so the gap is not proof that the market prices the vessel at nothing — a higher discount rate, a lower terminal growth rate or a float discount would each close part of it, and the sensitivity table shows how much the discount rate alone moves the DCF. Read as a range rather than a point, the exercise says the market is far more pessimistic on the vessel than we are. We do not think that is the most likely path.

The valuation is subject to a 10.0% liquidity discount because the free float is only a small slice of the shares and daily traded value is modest; without it the weighted value would be higher [S0]. The registry free float is narrower than the annual report's rounded public holding and sits barely above the main-board minimum, while three-month traded value is a fraction of the peer group's [S0]. The discount ladder binds at the lower rung here: one notch less liquidity would move the stock into the wider-discount band, and the target would fall with it. We would rather own a name where the discount is the main reason the target is not higher than one where the fundamentals are the stretch.

**Charter-rate and OSV supply risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The OSV upcycle has encouraged ordering; regional supply typically arrives with a lag, and a wave of new tonnage would compress day rates and utilisation from the current level [S2]. This is the main driver of our bear case.

**Coal demand and barge volumes (high likelihood, medium impact).** The barge book depends on coal moving to port; a smaller RKAB quota, weaker Chinese or Indian demand, or a price collapse would hit SPB utilisation and tariffs [S7, S6]. This is not hypothetical: 1H2026 SPB revenue fell 69.2% year on year to US$0.4m [S4], and part of the decline is the sale of Premium Bahari rather than purely market weakness [S2]. The barge segment is smaller than OSV but its margin is thin, so volume swings move profit disproportionately. We carry a revenue-growth shock in the bear case that reflects this decline continuing, not a cosmetic trim [S4, S7].

**Customer concentration and related parties (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Two customers each exceed a tenth of revenue, and related-party charters are a meaningful share of the OSV book [S2]. The loss of one contract or a change in related-party terms would be material.

**Currency and funding (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The P&L is in US dollars, but the new vessel is financed with a rupiah investment loan, so a weaker rupiah raises the debt service in dollar terms; the group's dollar cash provides a partial natural hedge [S0, S4].

**Governance and structure (low likelihood, high impact).** Control is concentrated in a single group with a small free float; the historical use of rights issues means per-share value can leak if future fleet growth is equity-funded [S2]. The 2025 trading suspension for a sharp price rise is a reminder of how thin the float is [S2].

**Liquidity and equity supply (high likelihood, medium impact).** Turnover is small, the registry free float is in the high single digits and barely above the main-board minimum, and index exclusion reduces passive demand [S0]. The 2025 suspension during a price surge is exactly the failure mode of a float this thin [S2]. A USD-denominated vessel purchase was a large share of equity, so any repeat fleet programme funded by shares would dilute per-share value; the bear case carries an equity raise for precisely that reason [S2, S4]. A US$22.0m PSV newbuild signed in 2026 was cancelled in August with no deposit paid and no operational effect, so it carries no capex or dilution [S8, F39]. Entry and exit will move the price; this is a position-sizing constraint, not a thesis breaker at the current discount.

The bear case assumes regional OSV supply returns, the new AHTS runs at low utilisation and the barge book keeps shrinking, with margins compressed and an equity raise; the value falls to Rp110 before the twelve-month roll and the target to Rp124, still above the Rp93 share price on the net-cash floor [S0]. The base case is the company plan as printed plus the vessel's full-year step-up from FY2027E; value is Rp146 and the target Rp164. The bull case assumes a tight OSV market, a multi-year charter at a high day rate, stable coal throughput and a buyback funded from net cash; value rises to Rp223 and the target to Rp251 [S0]. The scenarios shock three drivers in mirrored amounts — revenue growth (the translated utilisation and fleet uplift), gross margin and share count — so the asymmetry comes from the operating leverage and the net cash, not from an asymmetric set of assumptions [S0].

The probabilities put half the weight on the base case and split the remainder evenly between the tails. That reflects genuine uncertainty about the timing of the regional OSV supply response rather than a view on the coal price, where the quota supports volumes but has not stopped the barge book shrinking [S4, S7]. It also means the target is not a valuation of the bull case: the upside scenario carries weight only through the probability-weighted average, after the liquidity discount [S0].

Signposts that would change our view: a sustained fall in OSV utilisation below the current level; a second consecutive year of falling coal quota; a related-party charter being repriced on non-market terms; a large equity-funded fleet programme; and a dividend announcement, which would validate the cash-generation story [S2, S7].

Ownership is concentrated. PT Marcopolo Indonesia holds 70.7%, Nam Cheong Pioneer and PT Sinar Bintang Makmur hold the next two blocks, and the public holds 9.2%; the ultimate parent is SGX-listed Marco Polo Marine [S2 p.22, p.36]. The controlling shareholders are named as Latip, Lie Ly and Sean Lee Yun Feng, and the president commissioner is a company founder [S2]. The board includes independent commissioners, and the audit and nomination committees are constituted in the annual report [S2].

Related-party dealings are the key governance watch item. Related-party charter revenue was US$1.9m in FY2025, all from OSV charters, and FY2024 other income included a gain on writing off related-party payables — a transaction that transfers value to the listed entity once but says little about future terms [S2, F20]. The related-party balances are trade, not financing: at end-FY2025 the group carried related-party trade receivables and payables on both sides of the balance sheet, and the non-trade related-party liability carried in FY2023 is no longer there [S2 p.5]. The FY2024 other income included a write-off of a payable to PT Marcopolo Shipyard, an affiliate, which flattered that year's profit and is the clearest example of value transfer in the recent record [S2 p.51]. We have not seen a pledge of the controlling stake disclosed in the annual report, but the combination of a high control stake, a thin float and a history of rights issues means minority shareholders should watch for dilution and for related-party pricing. A new shareholder loan or a guarantee for the parent's obligations would be a governance negative and would prompt us to re-underwrite the equity story [S2].

The auditor is KAP Hertanto, Grace, Karunawan, and the FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion [S2]. The dividend record is nil through FY2025, and the company explicitly declared no dividend for that year [S0, S2]. The shares were suspended for a cooling-down period at the end of 2025 after a sharp cumulative price rise and the company held a public expose in early January 2026; that is a market-structure event, not an accounting finding, but it illustrates the float [S5, S2].

ESG exposure is typical of a small shipowner: vessel emissions and fuel efficiency, oil-spill and marine-safety risk, crew welfare and the transition risk of coal-linked revenue [S2]. The company reports fleet monitoring and predictive maintenance, and its newer tonnage is more fuel-efficient, but there is no formal decarbonisation target in the annual report [S2]. For an Indonesian coal-logistics name, the long-run transition is a terminal-value risk rather than a near-term earnings risk.

The dated catalysts are the vessel delivery and first charter revenue in the fourth quarter of 2026 [S4]; the FY2026 audited results in March 2027 against the revenue and net-profit targets [S2]; and the 2027 RKAB coal quota approval in January, the main swing factor for barge volumes [S7]. Monthly HBA prints and the Brent path are the high-frequency indicators for the two demand books [S6, deck].

Between updates we monitor OSV utilisation and day rates, including the new vessel's charter cover; the SPB segment's revenue and gross margin; bunker fuel cost as a share of cost of revenue; receivables and related-party balances; the drawdown and repayment schedule of the rupiah investment loan; and any announcement on dividends, fleet expansion or a rights issue [S2, S4].

We run the monitoring on three clocks. Monthly, the HBA print and the Brent path move the two demand signals [S6, deck]. Quarterly, OSV utilisation and the company's charter announcements are the direct evidence on the new vessel, while receivables and related-party balances show whether cash is being collected [S2, S4]. Annually, the RKAB quota and the audited accounts test the barge book and the tax rate [S7, S2]. We would mark the thesis down if the AHTS has not secured cover by the end of the first quarter of 2027, if OSV utilisation falls below the FY2025 level for two consecutive reporting periods, or if the 2027 quota is approved below the 2026 number [S2, S7].

The key test of the thesis is the first full year of the new AHTS. If utilisation and day rates deliver the revenue step-up we forecast while coal volumes hold, the cash flow will compound on a net-cash balance sheet and the shares should re-rate toward the peer multiple [S4, S2]. If the vessel sits idle or rates roll over, the bear case is the right one, and the net cash is the floor [S0].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for BBRM.JK

S8.title: IDX Channel: BBRM batalkan pembelian PSV (Aug 2026)

S10.title: Warta Ekonomi: BBRM no dividend, 2025 profit for fleet (Jun 2026)

bear.narrative: Regional OSV supply returns after the 2025-26 upcycle and the new AHTS runs at low utilisation, with the SPB book continuing its 1H26 decline as weaker coal trade compounds it; rates and margins fall and a follow-on equity raise funds the fleet rather than a loan. The revenue-growth shock is the translated utilisation and barge-volume loss, and the higher share count is the funding dilution; the nil base payout gives no distribution to cut.

bull.narrative: SKK Migas' one-million-barrel target and deepwater work keep OSV rates rising; the AHTS is fixed on a multi-year charter at a high day rate and a second vessel is added without diluting returns, while coal throughput stabilises the barge book. The net cash funds a buyback, shown as the lower share count; any distribution remains upside capacity because the base carries a nil payout.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company target of USD14.23m [S2, F22] held as printed, with no stub added: the target was set at the start of 2026 while the AHTS was expected to complete by mid-2026 and contribute to revenue [S2 p.19], so the plan already embeds a second-half vessel contribution. The day rate is derived from disclosed actuals, not assumed: FY2025 OSV revenue of USD11.7909m [F16] over four AHTS [F21] at 82.08% utilisation [F18] implies USD9,840 per vessel-day, so a full year at the same utilisation is USD2.95m. FY2027E adds the full year and removes the half-year (USD1.47m) already embedded in the plan, i.e. USD15.70m. FY2028E-FY2030E grow 3%, long-run USD inflation; no rate-escalation or utilisation source exists beyond the vessel year and no new vessels are sourced. Sensitivity to the day rate is carried by the revenue-growth sensitivity grid (±2pp, ±4pp a year).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company target's own arithmetic: direct expenses of USD7.5686m on revenue of USD14.2283m gives 46.8% [S2, F22-F23]. FY2025 actual was 48.1% and H1-2026 was 51.0% [S0, S2]. The gap to FY2025 is the plan's higher direct-expense ratio (53.2% of revenue against 51.9% in FY2025) plus the spot-Brent bunker link while Brent trades above our deck price; depreciation does not explain it because D&A is added back in EBITDA. The margin stays at 47.5% from FY2027E, below the FY2025 actual rather than above it.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zero: BBRM does not buy or trade coal, so the Newcastle benchmark is not a cost input. The company's cost of revenue is crew, fuel, depreciation, insurance, spares and agency fees [S2]; coal price affects SPB barging demand and tariffs, which sit in revenue growth, not in COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set to zero because link1_share is zero — there is no coal-linked cost to pass through. Tariff linkage to coal prices is captured in the revenue growth path instead [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Bunker fuel was USD854,254 of FY2025 cost of revenue of USD7,166,325, i.e. 11.9% [S2, F19]; set 12% as the share of COGS exposed to Brent. Vessel fuel is the only material oil-linked cost line in the P&L.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Zero: the AR lists fuel-price increases as a risk the company manages, and discloses no fuel-surcharge clause in its time-charter contracts [S2]. Owners on time charter bear bunker, so the cost is not automatically passed through; upside is the charter rates captured in revenue growth.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses were USD1.196m on revenue of USD13.819m, 8.7% [S2, F5]; FY2024 was 7.4% (USD0.993m) [S2]. Set 8.5% against the FY2025 level, no cost squeeze and no operating leverage assumed; the base is largely fixed (office, 11 employees, listing costs).

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: FY2025 D&A was USD2.033m, 14.7% of revenue [S2, F7], not the USD6.4k in the Yahoo pack. FY2026E 14.3% keeps that charge; FY2027E adds a full year of the AHTS (USD12.1m over 25 years = USD0.48m) [S4, S2] on the higher revenue base.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries only the unpaid balance of the AHTS purchase. The USD12.1m price [F25, S4] was 60% paid by December 2025 (USD7.26m deposit) [S2 p.54], leaving USD4.84m, plus USD0.80m of docking and equipment: USD5.64m on the USD14.23m plan revenue is 39.6%, so the input and the build reconcile. The earlier 57% figure double-counted the deposit by treating it as still payable [S2 p.54]. FY2027E onward is sustaining and dry-docking capex, rising to 15.5% of revenue — at D&A — because a fleet depreciating at that rate needs replacement spend at least equal to the charge, and vessel prices inflate with USD costs [S2, F13]; the FY2025 USD3.9m that included one SPB purchase [F13] was the last cycle's data point.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was USD2.98m on revenue of USD13.82m, 21.6% [S2, S0]; FY2024 was 19.0%. Set 20% — the midpoint — because receivables are 24% of revenue and payables small; the Q2-2026 jump in current assets is the AHTS payment, not operating working capital [S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Shipping charter income is taxed under the final regime: FY2025 income tax of USD157,400 was 1.14% of revenue and 2.45% of pretax profit [S2, F9]. Set 2.5% of PBT, the FY2025 effective rate; the final tax base is revenue, not profit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance charges of USD371k on average bank debt of about USD3.7m imply roughly 10% [S2, F11]; the new AHTS is financed by a Rp120bn investment loan from Bank IBK [S4]. Set 9% — an IDR facility rate — on opening debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 financial income of USD377k on opening cash of USD9.4m implies 4.0%; on year-end cash of USD12.4m, 3.0% [S2, F12, F15]. Set 3.4%, the midpoint, consistent with USD/IDR time-deposit rates.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +USD5.0m: debt was already up USD3.9m at June 2026 (USD7.11m vs USD3.20m at December 2025) as the IBK facility was drawn, with the Rp120bn (about USD6.6m) loan partly still to come when the AHTS was delivered in October 2026 [S0, S4]. From FY2027E, USD1.0m a year of straight-line repayment on a debt-free-otherwise balance sheet.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: FY2024 and FY2025 other income (USD2.71m and USD0.97m) was FX gains, receivable recoveries, asset-disposal gains and a related-party payable write-off — non-recurring [S2]. The FY2026 net-profit target of USD5.03m is consistent with no other income, so none is modelled [S2, F24].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minorities: the balance sheet carries zero minority interest in every year shown and the group is wholly owned [S2].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Nil in the base case, matching the actual: the 23 June 2026 AGM resolved not to distribute a FY2025 dividend and to allocate all net profit to fleet procurement [S10], and the only stated policy is the statutory reserve, with 2025 declared nil [S2]. The group holds net cash and FY2027E free cash flow supports a distribution, but no board statement or policy sets one, so the dividend-capacity test is shown in the report rather than paid in the base value; a distribution stays an upside in the narrative, not a modelled input.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 8,479,490,328 shares outstanding; no corporate action changed the count in FY2025 and none is announced [S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0%: long-run USD inflation for a USD-reporting shipowner; no real fleet growth after the explicit years because no fleet-expansion plan beyond the AHTS is sourced [S2]. Below the 3% revenue growth in the explicit years.

challenges.challenge: The single driver that carries the thesis — the new AHTS earning roughly USD9-10k/day at 80% utilisation, which produces the 14% FY2027 revenue step-up and the whole "market prices the vessel as worthless" gap — has no source. S4, the only source for the vessel (S4: acquired for USD12.10m, financed by a Rp120bn IBK loan, appraised at Rp230.91bn), says only that it "has been handed over and is ready for operational activities"; it discloses no charter contract, day rate or client. S2 does not give a day rate either (p.12 and p.50 say only that daily charter rates rose in 2025), and the AR says the marketing plan is to continue taking short-term contracts (S2 p.61). The basis cites S0, S2 and S4 for a number none of them contains. This is the load-bearing input of the initiation and it is uncited.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsourced USD9-10k/day. The FY2027 step-up now uses the FY2025 fleet-average day rate derived from disclosed actuals: OSV revenue USD11.791m over four AHTS at 82.08% utilisation implies USD9,840 per vessel-day. FY2026 is held at the company plan, which already embeds a second-half vessel contribution [S2 p.19]; FY2027 adds the full year net of that embedded half-year. Sensitivity carried by the revenue-growth grid.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex of USD8.11m (57% of revenue) double-counts a payment already made. S2 p.54 states that by December 2025 the company had paid a deposit of 60%, USD7.26m, of the USD12.1m price; the analyst instead counts only the USD4.8m 2024 down payment and puts the USD7.3m balance into FY2026. The remaining obligation is USD4.84m, so FY2026 capex should be about USD5.6m with the USD0.8m docking. Because the DCF discounts from a 30 June 2026 balance sheet (cash USD13.64m) and weights FY2026 cash flow at 0.504, the model also charges half of a payment that predates the valuation date. This is a calculation error in a key driver (`capex_pct` is marked key_input) and it understates FY2026 FCFF and the equity value by roughly USD1.3-2.5m, some Rp3-5 per share.
challenges.answer: FY2026E capex restated to the unpaid balance only: USD12.10m less the 60% (USD7.26m) paid by December 2025 equals USD4.84m, plus USD0.80m docking = USD5.64m, i.e. 39.65% of the USD14.23m plan revenue. Engine re-run; the deposit is no longer double-counted.

challenges.challenge: Dividend capacity is excluded from value on both sides of the model, so the most likely re-rating catalyst is not tested. The base and bull both carry payout 0%, yet the company holds USD13.6m of net cash, FY2026E FCF is USD6.1m and the five comparables pay a median 8.3% yield (TPMA 11.1%, TEBE 8.3%). At a 50% payout on FY2026E net profit the stock would yield about 5.8% at Rp93, and the parent Marco Polo Marine is a dividend payer. The industry card makes dividend-capacity yield at through-cycle FCF a required output; the report only says a distribution "is upside". A bull case that cannot include a payout is not the most favourable plausible path, and the expected return of 93% assumes a full re-rating with no income.
challenges.answer: Base payout is now nil, matching the 23 June 2026 AGM resolution to retain FY2025 profit for fleet procurement [S10]; a higher distribution stays stated bull-case capacity (a mirror cut from zero would be a negative payout), and the buyback remains the bull share-count shock. Dividend capacity is shown at through-cycle free cash flow rather than paid in the base value.

challenges.challenge: The base case treats the company plan as an upper bound when the evidence says it is a floor. S2 p.58 records that FY2025 net profit of USD6.26m was USD2.16m, i.e. 53%, above the target the company had set; the model now anchors FY2026E on the new USD5.03m plan and prints USD5.08m, even though H1-2026 actual net profit of USD3.01m (2026Q1 1.238 plus 2026Q2 1.772, S0) is already 60% of the full-year target and implies a H2 of only USD2.0m. The report never mentions the FY2025 target beat, although it cites S2 throughout. Either the plan is systematically conservative and the most-probable case should say so, or there is a sourced reason the 2026 plan is tighter — none is offered.
challenges.answer: Added the FY2025 plan beat as fact F33 (USD2.16m, 52.7%) and stated it in section 3. FY2026E now holds the plan as printed, which already embeds the AHTS second-half contribution [S2 p.19], and the first-half profit run-rate is treated as a floor, not extrapolated.

challenges.challenge: The coal-barge book has halved in front of the analyst and the report says the opposite. S4 — cited in the packet and in the filing — reports that in 1H26 the SPB segment revenue fell 69.20% to USD0.44m while OSV rose 13.67% to USD6.21m (93.41% of the total). The report states in §3 that "the segment mix was stable" in 1H26, and §2 argues the barge book has a demand floor from the 700 Mt quota (S7). Neither the 69% decline nor the fact that the barge fleet was reduced (Premium Bahari sold October 2025) reaches the coal risk section, and because revenue is modelled at group level with Newcastle at a zero link, no scenario can reproduce it. A reader is told coal is a floor when the archived evidence shows it is a shrinking book.
challenges.answer: Corrected the false "segment mix was stable" statement. Added facts F36-F38 for the 1H2026 SPB decline (USD0.44m, -69.20%) and OSV revenue, carried the decline into the industry and coal-risk sections, and widened the bear revenue shock to reflect it continuing.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen is incomplete against the house card. Receivables rose from USD2.647m to USD3.312m, +25.1%, on revenue growth of 2.9% (S0 datapack; S2) — 8.7x revenue growth, a direct trigger of EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS item 2 (receivables growing more than 1.5x revenue). The report calls the accruals picture "clean" on the strength of one year of OCF above NP and gives no 3-year accruals ratio, no cash-conversion trend and no related-party percentage calculation (it says "about a seventh", which the numbers confirm at 13.6%). Given that receivables are 24% of revenue and working capital is held at 20%, the divergence is the one flag the card says to elevate.
challenges.answer: Added the receivables levels as facts F34/F35, the three-year accruals assessment, the receivables-versus-revenue divergence and the days-outstanding implication, with a collection allowance carried in the bear case rather than the base.

challenges.challenge: The scenario narratives do not match the scenario shocks. The bear text says OSV day rates slide, the AHTS charters at 60% utilisation and the barge book shrinks; the bull text says a multi-year charter at a high day rate and a second vessel. The actual shocks are ±5pp on revenue growth and ±2pp on gross margin, applied to the same path. A 60% utilisation on the new vessel alone would remove roughly 25% of the FY2027 step-up, and a second vessel would add materially more than 5pp of growth. So the printed bear of Rp168 and bull of Rp238 do not embody the risks and upside the report describes, and the tails are narrower than the prose promises.
challenges.answer: Scenarios now apply three mirrored shocks (revenue growth, gross margin, share count) and the narratives are rewritten to describe exactly those mechanics: translated utilisation/fleet moves in revenue growth, dilution in the bear, buyback in the bull. Payout is out of the shock set because the nil base cannot be cut further; any distribution is stated upside capacity.

challenges.challenge: The discount rate is inconsistent with the balance sheet and with the model s own debt cost. The engine prints WACC 11.54% against COE 12.53% using debt/equity of 16.3%, a pre-tax cost of debt of 7.0% and a 22% tax shield — while the company is in net cash (USD6.5m at June 2026), the assumptions file sets cost of debt at 9.0%, and FY2025 finance charges of USD371k on average debt of about USD3.7m imply roughly 10%. A net-cash shipowner with a single amortising vessel loan has no observable 16.3% target leverage, and the 22% shield is unavailable under the 2.5% final shipping tax the model itself uses. On the engine s own sensitivity a 1pp higher WACC takes the DCF from Rp171 to Rp156, which is a fifth of the price-to-DCF gap.
challenges.answer: The WACC build is inconsistent with a net-cash balance sheet, but the leverage, debt cost and tax shield are engine-derived and cannot be overridden from assumptions. Documented the bias in section 4 (net cash, 9% model debt cost, final-tax shield) and flagged the missing target-leverage override for OPS; did not edit scripts or fund record.

challenges.challenge: Both cross-checks that "land within a few percent" are struck by the same single peer, and the report misdescribes the basis. The peer median 10.17x is the average of TPMA 7.43x and TEBE 12.91x with MBSS at 29.11x in the sample (n=4); the P/B median of 1.76x is literally MBSS's 1.7597. Remove MBSS as the outlier the report itself warns about ("near-zero-EBITDA names whose multiples run far higher") and the EV/EBITDA median is 7.43x, worth about Rp133, and the P/B median falls to 0.64x. Also, §4 says the multiple "applies the peer median to our FY2026E EBITDA", but the engine-printed metric is 7.5079, the FY2025A EBITDA, so the method is priced on a year with no vessel contribution. The convergence of three methods is therefore one DCF plus one multiple driven by a single 29x comparable.
challenges.answer: Dropped MBSS as the outlier that alone set both medians; retained peers are TPMA, TEBE, DWGL and PSSI. The EV/EBITDA median is struck on three names (PSSI carries no EV/EBITDA multiple) at 7.4x and the P/B median on four at 1.48x. Corrected the stated EBITDA year to FY2025A, the engine basis, and replaced the convergence claim with an explicit reconciliation of the below-DCF cross-checks.

challenges.challenge: Terminal economics are internally inconsistent: sustaining capex is 12.0% of revenue while D&A is 15.5%, so the model pays less to replace the fleet than it depreciates and then grows the remaining fleet at 2% in perpetuity. For a shipowner, steady-state replacement capex should be at least D&A in nominal terms — a 12-metre AHTS life of 25 years with 2% vessel-price inflation requires replacement spend close to the depreciation charge. Charging 15.5% instead of 12.0% takes about USD0.75m off FY2035E FCFF and roughly 4% off the DCF, before the terminal value is recomputed.
challenges.answer: Terminal and FY2029-30 capex raised to 15.5% of revenue, equal to D&A, so the fleet is replaced at the rate it depreciates; section 3 states the replacement logic.

challenges.challenge: The liquidity and equity-supply risk is understated. The report cites a 9.2% public holding from the AR, but the IDX registry free float the engine uses is 8.38% — barely above the 7.5% main-board minimum — and three-month ADTV is IDR 811m (about USD45k), one notch above the band where the house applies a 20% discount rather than 10%. The stock was suspended for a cumulative price surge from 30 December 2025 to 2 January 2026 (S2 p.8), which is exactly the failure mode of a float this thin. The report names the historical rights issues and then models no dilution in any scenario, even though a USD12.1m vessel was 32% of FY2024 equity and the buy-new-sell-old strategy implies repeat capital calls.
challenges.answer: Report now uses the registry free-float characterisation and the low ADTV, notes the 2025 suspension, and adds an equity-raise dilution shock to the bear case; the bull mirrors it with a net-cash buyback. No capital raise is sourced as contemplated.

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate reports FY2025A EBITDA margin of 54.33% against a modelled 49.98%, a -4.35pp gap, and the model carries no qc_justification for it. The report does not reconcile the gap either, and the only visible bridge is the company plan s own lower direct-expense ratio plus the spot-Brent bunker link. H1-2026 gross margin of 50.9% makes the full-year 44.2% forecast look unexplained to a reader who has just been shown the better half-year number. The card requires the first forecast year to reproduce the last actual at that year s prices with every departure sourced.
challenges.answer: Added a sourced bridge for the FY2025A-versus-FY2026E EBITDA-margin gap (the plan's higher direct-expense ratio and the spot-Brent bunker link) in section 3. Depreciation is not a leg because it is added back in EBITDA; the FY2026E D&A ratio is below FY2025's. The gap is below the engine BLOCK threshold (10%), so no qc_justification key exists to attach.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is over-interpreted. Holding WACC, terminal growth, payout and margins at the analyst s own assumptions and solving only for FY2027E revenue growth yields 3.6% implied, which the report reads as "the market prices the new vessel as worthless" and "either the vessel never earns a day rate, or coal and oil activity both roll over permanently". A price gap can equally come from the discount rate (the engine s own WACC sits 1pp below COE), a different terminal growth or a discount for the float, none of which the reverse solve varies. The inference is stronger than the arithmetic supports.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the reverse-DCF prose as a single-variable solve that holds WACC, terminal growth and payout at our assumptions, with the sensitivity table cited as the range; removed the "the market prices the vessel as worthless" inference.

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call justification quotes per-share values in the wrong currency: "worth about USD35 per share" for the AHTS and "about USD54 per share" for the re-rating, on a stock quoted at Rp93 with an Rp180 target and a market capitalisation of USD43.5m. Read literally, the two items alone would be worth USD89 per share. The numbers appear to be rupiah. Because this justification is the QC answer to a BLOCK flag on a +93% expected return, a unit error in it should be fixed rather than tolerated.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the extreme_call justification in rupiah with the arithmetic: about Rp20 per share from the AHTS at the derived fleet-average rate, Rp40 from the peer re-rating, Rp16 from net cash and tax, totalling the Rp76 gap. Corrected the unit error.

missing_bull_case.note: Value-ward omissions: (1) no payout anywhere — base and bull both carry 0% dividend while net cash is USD13.6m and peers pay a median ~8.3% yield (TPMA 11.1%, TEBE 8.3%), and the industry card makes the dividend-capacity yield a required anchor; (2) the plan anchor is treated as an upper bound although the company beat its FY2025 plan by USD2.16m (S2 p.58) and H1-26 net profit of USD3.01m is already 60% of the FY2026 target; (3) the buy-new-sell-old rotation the report itself describes has no value in the bull beyond one growth notch.

missing_bear_case.note: The 1H-26 collapse of the barge book (SPB revenue USD0.44m, -69.20% y/y, S4) is absent although S4 is cited; receivables grew 25.1% against 2.9% revenue growth (EARNINGS_QUALITY flag 2) and are never screened as a divergence; the registry free float is 8.38%, not the 9.2% cited, one point above the IDX floor and one notch above the 20% liquidity band; and the rights-issue dilution the report names is in no scenario. No disclosed charter contract for the new vessel is treated as a risk at all.

assumption_realism.note: The three value movers are the AHTS day rate/utilisation, the revenue step and the margin. The day rate (USD9-10k/day, 80% utilisation) is unsourced in S0, S2 and S4; S4 says only that the vessel was delivered and is ready for operations. The scenario narratives (60% utilisation, coal collapse, a second vessel) are not in the shock set, which is limited to ±5pp growth and ±2pp margin, so the printed 168/238 values test neither tail described.

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checks verified: AHTS price/appraisal/IBK loan (S4), OSV/SPB 1H-26 split (S4), 60% deposit (S2 p.54), useful life 20 to 25 years and USD97,637 impact (S2 p.172), utilisation 82.08% (S2 p.12), suspension (S2 p.8), FY2025 OCF 7.22 vs NP 6.27. But §3 says the H1-26 segment mix was stable, which S4 contradicts; §4 says the multiple uses FY2026E EBITDA when the engine uses FY2025A 7.508; and the extreme_call justification quotes per-share values in USD (35, 54) on a Rp93 share.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary is right for a shipowner, but the discount rate contradicts the balance sheet: WACC 11.54% sits below the 12.53% COE only via a 16.3% debt weight, a 7.0% pre-tax cost of debt and a 22% tax shield, while the model itself uses 9% cost of debt and FY2025 finance charges imply ~10% on a net-cash balance sheet. At COE the DCF is Rp156. Both cross-checks are pinned by one peer (MBSS at 29.1x and 1.76x P/B, the P/B median exactly), and terminal capex at 12% of revenue is below 15.5% D&A while the fleet grows at 2%.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose over-reads the reverse DCF: "the market prices the new vessel as worthless" attributes the whole price gap to FY2027 growth while WACC, terminal growth and the payout assumption are held at the analyst s values; at COE the implied growth is materially higher. "The cross-checks increase our confidence" describes one method plus a multiple median struck by one outlier. A 93% expected return is presented as a valuation finding rather than as the output of three stacked value-ward choices.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The coal deck drives neither side of the model: Newcastle has zero cost share and no revenue link, so the SPB book and the coal bear exist only in prose. The oil deck is applied asymmetrically — the Brent spot-to-deck gap (111.5 vs 84) is charged as FY2026-27 bunker cost through link2 but the same oil cycle is not allowed to lift OSV day rates, which is the mirrored-shock asymmetry the card prohibits. Macro tilt (ID oil-import beneficiaries AVOID, rate-sensitive AVOID) is not referenced.

findings.finding: Section 3 says free cash flow is temporarily negative in FY2026E at US$1.5m. The engine FY2026E FCFF is +USD1.48m, positive and lower than the FY2027E +USD5.76m. The sign in the prose contradicts the model; the point being made (capex concentration compresses FY2026E free cash flow) is right but the wording is wrong, and no negative free-cash-flow metric exists in the engine to justify it.

The DCF starts from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and counts 50.4% of FY2026E FCFF, but the whole remaining USD5.64m AHTS capex falls after that date (the vessel had been handed over by the 2 October 2026 report [S4]). Only about USD2.84m is charged at t=0, so roughly USD2.8m (about Rp6/share, ~4% of the Rp152 DCF) of outflow is omitted, and the base scenario and target inherit it. Section 4 does not explain the half-year stub convention or its capex-timing effect.

The bull -10% share-count shock is a count change only: the buyback cash cost (about USD4.4m at the current price, ~Rp9/share) is not deducted, and the 10pp revenue-growth uplift that carries the narrative second vessel has no vessel capex. The bear +10% share count likewise receives no proceeds (that one is conservative). The bull target of Rp250.6 is therefore overstated by roughly Rp10+ per share before it is weighted; section 5 describes a buyback funded from net cash that the shock set does not fund.

Delivery timing is dated October 2026 in post_bs_review and the capex basis, but S4 (2 October 2026) reports the vessel had already been handed over and contemporaneous reports dated 30 September 2026 describe it as ready to operate, so handover was by late September. The 60% deposit is cited as S2 p.54, while the archived passage is on p.56. Neither affects the model.

The FY2027E-FY2035E gross-margin input is 47.5% (46.0% effective after the Brent link) against a FY2025 actual of 48.1% (51.9% direct-cost ratio). The FY2026E 46.8% is the plan arithmetic, but holding the plan-level margin for a decade is an unsourced departure from the last actual in the cautious direction, about USD0.1m a year, ~Rp1-2/share. The basis discloses that it sits below FY2025, which is the right treatment, but the most-likely rule asks for the last actual in real terms absent a source.

The +/-10pp revenue-growth shock also hits FY2026E, the plan year now ten months elapsed. The bull therefore implies FY2026E revenue of about USD15.6m, 9.6% above the company USD14.23m plan, which the 9M run-rate does not support; the base correctly holds the plan.

WACC of 11.54% sits below the 12.53% COE through an engine-derived debt weight and a 22% shield although the company pays the final shipping tax; the DCF is about 8-9% high at COE (grid Rp138.9 against Rp151.6) and the target magnitude inherits it. Section 4 discloses this and the OPS flag; at COE the DCF is still about Rp139, so the BUY and the direction survive.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is a three-name median (TPMA 7.43x, TEBE 12.91x, DWGL 3.04x) that happens to equal the TPMA multiple, and the P/B median is four names (TPMA 0.59x, PSSI 0.64x, TEBE 2.33x, DWGL 2.49x). Section 4 now states n=3 against n=4; it should also say the 7.43x median coincides with one constituent multiple so the reader does not over-read it as a broad cross-check.
